reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / Low's Clinical Autonomic Disorders
clinicalPearls: Defined by a sustained rise in heart rate of at least 30 beats per minute (40 in adolescents) within ten minutes of standing or head-up tilt, without a significant fall in blood pressure
Symptoms of orthostatic intolerance include palpitations, light-headedness, tremulousness, blurred vision, fatigue, and cognitive 'brain fog', all relieved by lying down
Predominantly affects young women and frequently follows a viral illness, pregnancy, surgery, or trauma
Commonly overlaps with chronic fatigue, fibromyalgia, migraine, joint hypermobility (Ehlers-Danlos type), and gastrointestinal dysmotility
Recognised subtypes include hypovolaemic, neuropathic (partial dysautonomic), and hyperadrenergic forms that may coexist
An active-stand (lying-to-standing) test and head-up tilt confirm the heart-rate criterion; a symptomatic orthostatic tachycardia sustained over the recording period is required
Deconditioning perpetuates the syndrome, so prolonged bed rest should be avoided
Management is primarily non-pharmacological: volume and salt expansion, compression garments, physical counter-manoeuvres, graded exercise reconditioning, and avoidance of triggers
reference.pathophysiology: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome is a heterogeneous disorder of orthostatic intolerance in which assuming an upright posture provokes an exaggerated compensatory rise in heart rate without orthostatic hypotension. Several mechanisms may act, often in combination: reduced circulating blood volume, excessive venous pooling in the lower limbs and splanchnic bed, a partial peripheral autonomic (small-fibre) neuropathy that limits lower-body vasoconstriction, and a hyperadrenergic state with heightened central sympathetic outflow. Inadequate venous return lowers stroke volume, so heart rate rises steeply to preserve cerebral perfusion, generating the characteristic symptoms. Physical deconditioning and abnormal fluid regulation frequently perpetuate the cycle.
additionalDifferentials: Orthostatic hypotension due to autonomic failure
additionalInvestigations: Active-stand (lying-to-standing) test with serial heart rate and blood pressure over ten minutes
Head-up tilt-table testing where the active-stand test is equivocal
Full blood count and thyroid function to exclude anaemia and thyrotoxicosis
Supine and standing plasma catecholamines when a hyperadrenergic subtype is suspected
Ambulatory ECG monitoring to exclude a primary arrhythmia
Autonomic function testing including QSART where available
redFlags: Syncope on exertion or causing injury, suggesting a cardiac cause
A significant orthostatic fall in blood pressure indicating autonomic failure rather than POTS
Features of phaeochromocytoma such as paroxysmal hypertension, headache, and sweating
Progressive neurological signs suggesting a wider autonomic neuropathy
reference.prognosis: Many patients, particularly those with a post-viral onset, improve substantially over months to years with reconditioning and non-pharmacological measures, although a proportion have persistent, disabling symptoms that require long-term multidisciplinary support.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the orthostatic tachycardia as anxiety and overlooking the reproducible heart-rate criterion
Diagnosing POTS when an orthostatic fall in blood pressure actually indicates orthostatic hypotension
Failing to exclude dehydration, anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, or medication effects before making the diagnosis
Recommending prolonged rest, which worsens deconditioning and perpetuates symptoms
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: First-line non-pharmacological volume support with increased salt and fluid intake plus lower-limb and abdominal compression garments to counter venous pooling
Structured graded reconditioning programme beginning with recumbent or semi-recumbent exercise to reverse deconditioning
Heart-rate control with a beta-blocker or ivabradine for symptomatic orthostatic tachycardia
Fludrocortisone for volume expansion and midodrine for vasoconstriction in hypovolaemic and neuropathic subtypes, with pyridostigmine where autonomic neuropathy predominates
Withdraw aggravating agents and treat coexisting conditions such as anaemia, migraine and gastrointestinal dysmotility
Educate on trigger avoidance (prolonged standing, heat, large carbohydrate meals) and physical counter-manoeuvres
Multidisciplinary support involving autonomic specialists, cardiology and physiotherapy for persistent, disabling symptoms
